cards.back: The value a function approaches as its input approaches a specified point.
A first-order local approximation f(a+h) ≈ f(a) + f′(a)h.
The derivative rule for nested functions: d f(g(x))/dx = f′(g(x))g′(x).
The local derivative of an output with respect to a modeled input.
An interior candidate for an extremum where a derivative is zero or undefined.
The set of inputs that satisfy a model's physical and design constraints.
The signed accumulation of a quantity over an interval.
The result linking derivatives and integrals: accumulation can be evaluated using an antiderivative.
dN/dt = rN, N = N₀e^(rt); r = ln 2 / t_d is per-capita, units 1/time.
ln N is linear in t: r = ln(N₂/N₁)/(t₂ − t₁); more points test whether growth is exponential.
dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K) peaks at N = K/2 with rate rK/4: the inflection point of the S-curve.

cards.front: Time to a fraction of K
cards.back: t = (1/r) ln[(p/(1 − p))((K − N₀)/N₀)]; approach to K slows sharply.
V_max S/(K_m + S) → V_max as S → ∞, never reached at finite S; 99% needs S = 99 K_m.
v′(0) = lim (v(h) − v(0))/h = V_max/K_m; linear error is S/K_m.
∫ₐᵇ r dt = F(b) − F(a): net change of the quantity whose rate is r.
Total moved is ∫|r| dt; split where the rate changes sign.
A limit describes nearby values. Continuity also requires that the function is defined and its value equals that limit.
For every positive output tolerance ε, choose a positive input radius δ that guarantees the required closeness on the punctured neighborhood.
f′(a)=lim_(h→0)[f(a+h)−f(a)]/h. A finite derivative implies continuity, but a continuous corner can lack a derivative.
A finite table suggests behavior. Algebra and assumptions are needed to establish the limit; cancellation can spoil tiny-step calculations.
Differentiate the outer function and multiply by the inner derivative; intermediate units cancel.
Differentiate y as a dependent function. The formula dy/dx=−x/y for a circle requires y≠0.
Differentiate the constraint before substituting instantaneous values. Include every changing factor.
dy/dx and dy/dt answer different questions. Their relationship requires dx/dt and a valid local dependency.
The sign of f′ controls increase/decrease; the sign of f″ controls concavity. Zeros alone do not certify extrema or inflections.
For a continuous function on a closed bounded interval, compare feasible interior critical points and endpoints; optima can tie.
Express the objective in one feasible variable before differentiating. Discard infeasible stationary candidates.
An optimum belongs to the stated objective and constraints; changing the cost or feasible set changes the problem.
A definite integral of a rate is signed net change with rate×input units. Add an initial state to obtain the final state.
d/dt ∫_(a(t))^(b(t))v(s)ds=v(b(t))b′(t)−v(a(t))a′(t), under the stated smoothness conditions.
Change the integrand, differential and endpoint bounds consistently. Differentiate an antiderivative to check the chain factor.
The time average is the definite integral divided by interval length. It need not equal the midpoint rate.
[f(t+h)−f(t−h)]/(2h) has leading smooth truncation error proportional to h², but measurement error can be amplified by 1/h.
Trapezoids integrate straight chords; Simpson uses 1,4,2,...,4,1 weights on an even number of uniform panels.
Trapezoid error≤LM₂h²/12; Simpson error≤LM₄h⁴/180, with derivative bounds across the interval and their required smoothness.
Separate truncation, rounding, measurement and model error. A deterministic bound is not a standard deviation.
f(a+h)≈f(a)+f′(a)h; if |f″|≤M throughout the connecting interval, the error is at most Mh²/2.
x_(n+1)=x_n−f(x_n)/f′(x_n). Check nonzero derivative, domain and convergence evidence.
For nonzero reference input/output, E=(x/f)f′ is dimensionless and δf/f≈Eδx/x locally.
Tangent approximations and Newton convergence are local statements. They do not supply global accuracy or extend a function domain.
ln(C/C₀)=−kt for a single exponential; a base-10 slope is −k/ln 10. State the base and time units.
For Y=C+B, d ln Y/dt=−kC/(C+B). A positive constant background flattens the logarithmic curve.
Mixed rates, background and sensor dynamics can produce similar curvature. Independent evidence is needed to identify the cause.
Use positive dimensionless log ratios, state corrections and uncertainty, and reserve independent observations for prediction checks.
For positive exponential values, k=ln(C₁/C₂)/(t₂−t₁). Two points give an apparent rate, not a model-shape test.
Subtract a justified additive background before logging; ln(C+B) is not ln C+ln B. Propagate correction uncertainty.
Fit and tune on the specified early window, then compare predictions with reserved later observations.
Balanced offsets simplify the lab; they do not establish a real noise distribution or independent experimental replication.
